problem.title: Card-fraud scoring service
problem.context: A payments company scores about 3,000 card transactions per second, with seasonal peaks of 15,000. Fraud patterns adapt within weeks and confirmed chargeback labels arrive days to weeks later. Auditors may ask months later why a score was produced. Five data scientists, two ML engineers and the operations team run the system; there is no ML platform team.

requirements.text: Score every card transaction before the authorization decision, using the cardholder's recent activity (for example, the spending of the last hour and the last day).
Update the model as new confirmed fraud cases arrive.
For any past score, show which model version and which input values produced it.
During a seasonal peak of 15,000 transactions per second, a score comes back within 30 ms at the 99th percentile.
When the scoring service or one of its data sources fails, authorizations go on. The business accepts weaker fraud detection for up to 15 minutes, but no authorization may fail because of scoring.
An auditor asks about a score from up to 13 months ago. Within one working day the team answers with the model version, the input values and the training data that model was built from.
When the fraud loss rate rises in one segment, a retrained model can be in production within 48 hours, after it has been compared with the current model on recent transactions.
Card data must stay inside the company's PCI-certified environment: no external service may process it.
Seven people build and run the system, with no dedicated ML platform team.

approaches.idea: What if streaming features and automated challenger evaluation keep up with rapidly changing fraud?
What if colocated rolling state and scheduled operator routines keep the system small enough for seven people?
What if a replayable internal event ledger is the primary source for feature reconstruction and audit?
What if shared relational feature tables offer a familiar operational center for a small team?

values: Feature state: Stream-maintained online store
Serving: Redundant scorer with local fallback
Model release: Automated champion-challenger pipeline
Audit evidence: Immutable per-score record and versioned training snapshot
trajectory.hypothesis: Streaming state and redundant scorers should meet peak latency and fail-open needs (Q1,Q2); automated comparison should support the 48-hour update goal (R2,Q4), while immutable records support retrospective evidence (R3,Q3).
trajectory.observation: The combination covers the functional and service scenarios if all components stay internal, but the streaming platform and automated pipeline add work for a team without platform specialists.

values: Feature state: Per-scorer rolling state
Serving: Scorer colocated with per-node state
Model release: Scheduled batch retraining with operator promotion
Audit evidence: Per-score record plus versioned feature/model artifacts
trajectory.hypothesis: Local rolling state and a colocated scorer should keep common feature reads fast and remove a remote feature-store dependency (R1,Q1,Q2); scheduled promotion is operationally simple, though the 48-hour target needs discipline (R2,Q4).
trajectory.observation: This is light to operate and fast on healthy nodes, but replicas can diverge or lose recent state, and ordinary versioned artifacts need explicit retention and training-set lineage to satisfy the long audit window.

values: Feature state: Replayable internal transaction log
Serving: Scorer over materialized replay state
Model release: Human-reviewed candidate promotion
Audit evidence: Replayable event and model lineage ledger
trajectory.hypothesis: An internal replay log should reconstruct recent features and preserve long-term evidence (R1,R3,Q3); materialized state is needed for low latency, and human comparison can govern release (R2,Q4).
trajectory.observation: Replay and lineage make audits compelling, but replay infrastructure and human release gates create operational load and uncertain peak latency and update timing.

values: Feature state: Stream-maintained online store
Serving: Redundant scorer with local fallback
Model release: Scheduled batch retraining with operator promotion

trajectory.hypothesis: Replace continuous automated release with a scheduled, operator-promoted process while retaining the scalable feature and fallback path; this should improve C2 while keeping Q1, Q2 and Q3, with Q4 dependent on a tightly timed cadence.
trajectory.observation: Scheduled retraining better fits team capacity, but a slow review cadence may miss the 48-hour adaptation window.

values: Feature state: Per-scorer rolling state

trajectory.hypothesis: Strengthen per-score audit retention and training-set provenance without adding a shared serving dependency; this should improve R3 and Q3 while retaining the small-team fit.
trajectory.observation: The audit gap can be closed with retained records, but local state replication and fail-open behavior remain the weak points.

values: Feature state: Replayable internal transaction log

trajectory.hypothesis: Use scheduled operator promotion rather than a bespoke human gate to keep the event ledger while reducing operational ceremony; Q4 may remain only partial.
trajectory.observation: The audit strength survives the simpler release workflow, but the event path still has substantial run and recovery demands.

values: Feature state: Shared relational feature tables

trajectory.hypothesis: A familiar internal database with redundant scorers may be easier for operations to run than a streaming platform (C1,C2), though database contention may constrain Q1 at peak.
trajectory.observation: Familiar operations help staffing and redundant scoring helps availability, but shared database capacity and complete long-term lineage need careful limits.

trajectory.hypothesis: Restore automated comparison and promotion to address the 48-hour constraint while retaining streaming capacity, redundant fallback and explicit input/model artifacts; the tradeoff is greater C2 burden.
trajectory.observation: Automation resolves the update-timing weakness; the remaining concern is whether the team can own the additional platform components.

values: Feature state: Per-scorer rolling state
Serving: Scorer colocated with per-node state
Model release: Automated champion-challenger pipeline
Audit evidence: Per-score record plus versioned feature/model artifacts
trajectory.hypothesis: Automate recent-transaction comparisons and promotion so the light local-state design can meet the 48-hour update window; this improves Q4 at added C2 cost.
trajectory.observation: Automation addresses adaptation speed and explicit artifacts answer audits, while local failure handling and pipeline ownership remain concerns.

trajectory.hypothesis: Add redundant scorer instances with local fallback around the replay-derived state to improve Q2 while retaining replayable lineage; Q1 depends on materialized state rather than synchronous replay.
trajectory.observation: Fallback removes authorization dependence on one scorer or source and the ledger remains auditable, although log operations and human review still require capacity.

trajectory.observation: Durable snapshots address audit needs, but database peak capacity and scheduled promotion still leave latency and adaptation headroom uncertain.

alternatives.name: Streaming and automated
alternatives.summary: Use an internal streaming feature path, redundant scoring with local fallback, automated challenger evaluation, and retained score and training evidence. It covers the service targets well, with higher platform ownership demands.

choices.reason: Continuously maintained recent features keep the scoring path suitable for high transaction volume.

choices.value_id: Serving: Redundant scorer with local fallback
choices.reason: Redundant instances and a local fallback keep authorization independent of a failed scorer or source.
Automated comparison and release support updates within the required window.

choices.value_id: Audit evidence: Per-score record plus versioned feature/model artifacts
choices.reason: Each score records its inputs and model references, and versioned artifacts preserve training provenance.

considered.value_id: Model release: Scheduled batch retraining with operator promotion
considered.reason: This lowered platform burden but left the 48-hour adaptation target only partly met.

alternatives.name: Local state with automated release
alternatives.summary: Keep recent features beside each scorer and automate candidate comparisons and promotion. This limits shared serving infrastructure and retains explicit per-score artifacts, but depends on careful local-state recovery and pipeline ownership.

choices.reason: Local activity windows avoid a remote lookup on the scoring path, with bounded replication needed for failover.

choices.value_id: Serving: Scorer colocated with per-node state

Automated comparison addresses the update deadline that scheduled manual promotion could miss.

choices.value_id: Audit evidence: Per-score record plus versioned feature/model artifacts

choices.value_id: Serving: Redundant scorer with local fallback

adrs.title: Maintain recent transaction features for scoring
adrs.context: Recent cardholder activity must be available before authorization at peak load. The serving path must stay inside the PCI environment and tolerate component or source failures, while remaining operable by a small team.

Redundant scoring and fallback preserve authorization availability.
cons: Streaming and online-state operations add platform ownership.
options.reason: A1 prioritizes peak capacity and fail-open behavior, accepting additional operational burden.

adrs.title: Compare and promote updated fraud models
adrs.context: Chargeback labels arrive late, but segment loss can rise quickly. Candidate models must be compared with recent transactions and reach production within 48 hours, using a process seven people can run.

options.name: Automated champion-challenger release
values: Model release: Automated champion-challenger pipeline
pros: Automates comparison against the current model.
Supports a repeatable release within the adaptation window.
cons: Pipeline reliability and governance need engineering ownership.
options.reason: A1 and B1 use automation to address the 48-hour requirement despite higher ownership cost.

options.name: Scheduled operator promotion
values: Model release: Scheduled batch retraining with operator promotion
pros: Fits familiar batch operations and explicit operator control.
cons: A sparse or delayed schedule can exceed the production deadline.
options.reason: D1 accepts timing risk to keep model operations straightforward.

options.name: Human-reviewed promotion
values: Model release: Human-reviewed candidate promotion
pros: Makes candidate comparison and release review explicit.
cons: Availability of reviewers can delay production beyond 48 hours.
options.reason: C1 favors deliberate review for a ledger-centered system and needs a rapid review process.

adrs.title: Retain evidence for past scores and model training
adrs.context: For up to 13 months, the team must connect any score to its model and exact input values and identify the training data behind that model. Evidence must remain inside the PCI environment and be retrievable within one working day.

options.name: Per-score artifacts
values: Audit evidence: Per-score record plus versioned feature/model artifacts
pros: Directly links each score to exact input and model versions.
cons: Retention and indexing must cover the full audit window.
options.reason: A1 and B1 retain evidence next to the decision with artifact version references.

options.name: Replayable lineage ledger
values: Audit evidence: Replayable event and model lineage ledger
pros: Supports reconstruction and training lineage queries.
cons: Requires durable log retention and replay expertise.
options.reason: C1 uses the ledger as the primary historical record.

options.name: Immutable score and training snapshots
values: Audit evidence: Immutable per-score record and versioned training snapshot
pros: Preserves exact inputs and training snapshot references.
cons: Snapshot storage, cataloging and retrieval need operational discipline.
options.reason: D1 chooses explicit snapshots that complement a shared relational feature store.
